name: Kyrgyzstan
summary: A mountain country of nomadic heritage; Soviet until 1991; several revolutions since 2005.

knownFor.label: Manas epic
knownFor.note: One of the longest epic poems.

terrain.value: Over 90% mountains, mainly the Tian Shan and Pamir-Alay, with the large Lake Issyk-Kul and part of the Fergana Valley.

climate.value: Continental: cold, snowy winters and warm, dry summers, with much colder conditions high in the mountains.

resources.value: Gold (the Kumtor mine), hydropower from the Naryn River and Toktogul dam, coal, and pasture for herds.

disasters.value: Earthquakes, mudflows, landslides and avalanches; Soviet-era uranium waste at Mailuu-Suu is a pollution risk.

urbanisation.value: About a third of people live in towns; Bishkek, the capital, has around a million and Osh is the second city.

disease.value: Tuberculosis and other infections remain problems; health care is weaker in remote mountain areas.

migration.value: Hundreds of thousands work abroad, mostly in Russia and Kazakhstan; many ethnic Russians and Germans left in the 1990s.

economicBase.value: Gold (the Kumtor mine and other regions) and remittances, which are currently about 15% of GDP, down from a high of 35%. Livestock and re-exports are not mentioned in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Mountain passes to China such as Torugart and Irkeshtam; Bishkek’s Dordoi bazaar re-sells Chinese goods across the region.

moneyAndTax.value: The som, introduced in 1993, when Kyrgyzstan was the first Central Asian state to leave the Russian rouble zone.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic; it reverted to a presidential system in 2021.

keyRulers.value: Kyrgyzstan’s presidents since independence in 1991 are not named here; several were ousted by protests (2005, 2010).

succession.value: Presidents are elected, but popular uprisings forced presidents from power in 2005, 2010 and 2020.

institutions.value: The Jogorku Kenesh (parliament), the presidency and courts, under constitutions changed in 2010 and 2021.

stability.value: Tulip Revolution: a bloodless coup on 24 March 2005; protests in April 2010 against President Bakiyev.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Small armed forces; Russia has kept an air base at Kant since 2003, and the US used Manas airbase from 2001 to 2014.

majorWars.value: No major wars. Clashes between Kyrgyz and Uzbek communities in Osh and Jalal-Abad in June 2010 caused over 400 deaths. Protests ousted the president in 2005, 2010 and 2020. The Tajikistan border clashes are not covered by the part of the page read.

territoryChange.value: Borders inherited from the Soviet Union; long-disputed lines were settled by treaties with Uzbekistan (2023) and Tajikistan (2025).

alliancesRivals.value: A member of the Russian-led CSTO and Eurasian Economic Union (2015) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Near-universal literacy from Soviet schooling; universities include Kyrgyz National University and the American University of Central Asia.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Mountain highways such as the Bishkek–Osh road, few railways, and international airports at Bishkek and Osh.

religion.value: About 91% Muslim in the infobox (2026); the text cites 90% (CIA, 2017) and 86.3% (Pew, 2009).

languageWriting.value: Kyrgyz is the state language and Russian is official; both are written in the Cyrillic alphabet.

artsArchitecture.value: Shyrdak felt carpets, decorated yurts, the long oral Manas epic and music on the three-stringed komuz.

socialStructure.value: Kyrgyz about three-quarters of the population, Uzbeks about one-seventh mainly in the south, plus Russians and others.

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in nomadic heritage, the Manas epic and the yurt; the yurt’s roof ring (tunduk) is on the national flag.

dailyLife.value: Many families raise sheep and horses and take herds to summer pastures; beshbarmak and kymyz (mare’s milk) are traditional.

ideasReligions.value: A revival of Islam since 1991, alongside interest in Tengrism, the old Turkic sky religion, and Soviet secular habits.

colonisation.value: Part of the Russian Empire from the 1800s and the Soviet Union from the 1920s until 1991.

riseSignals.value: Formally incorporated into the Russian Empire in 1876 (then called Kirghizia); joined the Mongol Empire peacefully in 1207.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; it has been one of the more open political systems in Central Asia, though also unstable.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Kirghiz SSR established on 5 December 1936; independence declared on 31 August 1991.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
